text:
He saw her bent over the washbasin, cooling her face; he imagined that, out of some feminine coquetry, she powdered herself all over before going to bed. That soft scent of the powder and of her perfumed skin, mingled together, breathed beneath his nostrils like a living thing. And he saw her sit down beside the bed, stretch a little in her languor, in the delight of imminent rest, cross one leg over the other to take off her little shoe, let it fall upon the bedside rug, then slowly roll the very fine black stocking down her calf, and the small foot emerge from it, polished like an ivory jewel, restless in its slender shape, nervous as a hand. Linger a little as she likewise took off the other little shoe, the other stocking, look around with that listless gaze of a woman who would not wish to sleep alone, then rise, take from atop the coverlet a beautiful nightgown all lace and ribbons, lay it out with a few caressing movements, unfasten the one she wore and let it slip down like a sheath, with a slow smile....

She would go to look in the mirror one last time, then go to bed.

He pictured these things minutely, agonizingly, like someone drinking an exquisite poison in little sips. The tepid night swathed him in scents too strong; an indefinable silence full of agitation hung between heaven and earth; the hidden nocturnal life multiplied around him in the drunken garden.

Through the foliage of the trees he gazed with a kind of stupefaction at that lighted window on the first-floor terrace.

Suddenly, he could no longer withstand those visions; he crossed the garden in haste and went upstairs.

She had gone out onto the deserted terrace, had stretched out languidly in the reclining chair, and was now waiting for him, gazing into the miracle of the night, where the magnificence of the stars trembled with a kind of furious intensity.

“What are you doing out there? Haven’t you gone to bed, then?”

A little intoxicated by the stars, by the silence, and by love, she held out both arms to him without answering.

“Why don’t you undress?” he asked again.

“I was waiting for you,” she replied in a slow, slightly veiled voice.

The light breath of night had passed through her hair; the whiteness of the moonbeam shone upon her face. “It is damp in the evening,” he observed; “do not stay outside too long.”

Then, turning quickly, he said to her, “It is late now; sleep well. Farewell.”

“Rigo...” she uttered softly, as though she were still lost in the dream. And there was a little intoxication in her feminine languor, in her ambiguous manner, in the voice with which she called him. “Rigo, come here: sit down.”

She made a little room for him beside her. He obeyed silently. The warmth of that sweet body spread through his veins like a poisoned, exceedingly slow pleasure. He was bent over her face; the girl’s hands caressed his hair, his forehead.

Then she began to speak to him softly, with long pauses, trembling.

“You must not leave me alone.... Tonight more than ever I feel the need to be close to you, very close, because it would be truly melancholy to put a wall, to close a door, between you and me.... Do you not see what a magnificent night it is? There is a scent of jasmine drifting through the air like an intoxicating powder. And then I feel so full of torpor tonight.... Kiss me!... My hands are hot, feel.... They hurt.... They burn. I want to stay here all night, talking to you, caressing you, rather than remain alone.”

She thrust her fingers into his thick hair, as one sometimes does into warm furs in winter. And she continued:

“Down there, in the garden, you said such grave things to me that I am troubled by them; I should like to weep, but in the depths of my heart there is a joy that laughs, a kind of inexpressible hope.... Do not leave me alone. Or I should even like to do something I have never done: come into your bed, fall asleep beside you.... Kiss me! And then tell me something truly dangerous.... Even an innocent word, if you do not wish to tell me anything else.... I love you, and alone I shall not be able to sleep... because I want you to kiss me. Feel how much in love my mouth is.... Kiss me! I am yours... yours... take me! I desire nothing but to suffer from you... for you.... Hurt me a little... give me a kiss, only one, without end... bend down....”

These words, spoken close to his mouth, lulled him like the music of a sweet enchantment, swathed his aching senses in ineffable relief, and, closing his eyes, he stiffened in order to listen to her. A great shudder of pleasure passed over his cold flesh; an imperceptible wasting, an endless yearning spread through him beneath the caress of that voice.

She spoke again, enervated, exhausted:

“Look: I am closing my eyes... I am asleep. Bend down a little, kiss me!... I am so sleepy... I love you. Be gentle with me.... Listen: there is no sound, no one is watching us... kiss me!”

Like a madman he kissed her mouth, her forehead, her temples, her neck, her wrists, her hands, with a hoarse pant in his constricted throat, and he kissed her all over her perfumed flesh until his breath failed him. Then he rose, his hair disheveled, tore himself free from her as she held him, thrust her violently back upon the cushions, ran into his own room, and locked himself in.

She gave a little cry and, still quivering beneath the scourge of those kisses, burst into a convulsion of tears, then for a few moments remained almost lifeless.

The half-moon was rising above the mountains, high, clear, far from the stars.

He flung himself onto the bed, biting the pillows, clutching at the covers, to master the tumult that was rending him within, and not to hear that hushed voice pleading with him from behind the door, and not to look any further into the terrible possibility of that hour.

The night advanced, clear, almost trembling, toward the heights of its glorious radiance, strewing across the vault of infinity a still greater magnificence of stars. The lake and the shores, inhabited by the shadows of night, pervaded by the ambiguity of silence, clothed themselves in white splendors beneath the enchantment of the night.

A span of time passed that seemed infinite to him; then he thought he understood that she had begun to undress. He no longer heard upon the floor the sound of her slender heels, but the soft tread of two slippers moving hurriedly; then he was tempted to go to the inner door that separated them and listen. But instead the door to the corridor suddenly opened, and she entered.

She was in a dressing gown, frightened, pale, and stopped on the threshold. He sprang down from the bed and stood staring at her in astonishment.

“What do you want?...” he stammered in a choked voice.

“Nothing,” she replied. She looked at him. There was an unfamiliar light in her altered eyes; the expression of that face was singularly changed. There was something harsh and wild in her too, in her mouth, usually so smiling.

“Will you not sleep tonight?”

“No.”

Then her brother began to pace gloomily about the room, without going near her, as though he were contemplating some horrible act against her.

But abruptly he opened the window and went out onto the terrace.
